analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on corporations and wealthy individuals hiding money in offshore tax havens.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 32 House Democrats, never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Treasury Department new power to restrict foreign jurisdictions and banks that block U.S. tax enforcement [S2]. It expands reporting of foreign accounts, lets the IRS presume money moved through banks that refuse to report is taxable income, makes some foreign corporations managed from the U.S. pay domestic taxes, taxes offshore swap payments, and lowers the income threshold for the corporate minimum tax on companies that shift profits abroad [S2]. It would also force public companies to disclose what they pay in taxes, country by country [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently shoulder more of the tax burden when corporations and wealthy individuals shift income offshore; the Treasury, which would gain new tools to collect; and domestic businesses that compete against multinationals using tax havens.

how_it_helps.text: Requires public companies to disclose profits and taxes paid on a country-by-country basis, so investors and the public can see when profits are booked in low-tax havens [S2].

Lets the Treasury impose restrictions on foreign jurisdictions and financial institutions that significantly impede U.S. tax enforcement, including banning correspondent accounts and card processing [S2].

Creates a presumption that money routed through banks that refuse to comply with foreign-account reporting rules is taxable income or controlled by the U.S. person involved, unless the taxpayer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence [S3].
Lowers the gross receipts threshold for the base erosion and anti-abuse tax from $500 million to $100 million, so more multinational companies face the minimum tax on profits shifted abroad [S2].
Treats certain foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations, and taxes swap payments sent offshore as U.S.-source income [S2].
Subjects investment advisers and company formation agents to anti-money laundering rules, closing a channel used to create anonymous shell companies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits offshore, oil and gas companies using foreign structures, offshore banks and financial institutions, investment advisers and formation agents facing new compliance rules, and wealthy individuals with hidden foreign accounts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose significant new reporting and compliance costs on companies with foreign operations and on financial institutions, costs that could be passed on to customers [S3].

The new presumptions would shift the burden of proof onto taxpayers who use foreign institutions, who could only rebut them with clear and convincing evidence — a heavy standard that could sweep in legitimate cross-border transactions along with evasion [S3].
Lowering the corporate minimum tax threshold to $100 million in gross receipts would pull mid-sized companies into a complex anti-abuse regime designed for the largest multinationals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose — making it harder to hide corporate profits and personal wealth offshore — serves ordinary taxpayers directly, since the money they currently make up comes back. The heaviest costs fall on large multinationals and the offshore financial industry, not on most households. The legitimate complaints are the compliance burden on mid-sized companies and the aggressive burden-shifting in the new evidentiary presumptions, which a careful version of the bill could have narrowed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services Committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on March 11, 2021 [S1].
The bill had 32 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in the bill's action history; the House never considered it [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and the offshore financial services industry came out ahead: they avoid the new disclosure requirements, taxes on offshore profits, and anti-money laundering rules the bill would have imposed. Ordinary taxpayers continue to cover the share of the tax burden those actors shift offshore.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end offshore corporate tax avoidance

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Richard Neal)
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral, so it never advanced

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee with partial jurisdiction over the disclosure and anti-money-laundering provisions
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored the bill; because it never reached a vote, no roll-call breakdown exists [S4].

industries.note: The bill repeals check-the-box rules, taxes offshore swap payments, tightens the corporate minimum tax, and requires public country-by-country disclosure of profits and taxes [S2][S3]. These companies' ability to shift profits offshore is paid for through higher taxes on everyone else.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and tax-haven financial institutions
industries.note: Treasury could restrict or cut off jurisdictions and banks that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and money routed through banks that refuse reporting rules would be presumed taxable income [S2][S3]. These institutions profit from secrecy that shields tax evasion.

Foreign base-company oil income would become immediately taxable, and companies paying foreign levies while receiving economic benefits from those countries could no longer credit the full amounts [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Investment advisers and company formation agents
industries.note: New deadlines would require anti-money laundering programs, suspicious activity reports, and customer identification rules for advisers and for firms that create shell corporations [S2][S3]. These businesses profit from the anonymity the bill targets.
